What are treats? Facts about food treats
 Used as training aids or rewards for good behaviour.
 Provide enrichment and mental stimulation.
 May strengthen the bond with your dog.
 Too many treats can be harmful if they:
x unbalance the main diet
x contribute to unintended weight gain
Developing healthy treating habits
 Supervise your dog with chews, treats and toys.
www.wsava.org Transforming Care Together
Feeding treats to your dog
Unsafe treats
 Bones (cooked and raw) can be very dangerous and cause significant damage if chewed and/or ingested by dogs.5
 Excessively hard chews and treats, for example, antlers and hooves, and those with sharp edges should be avoided.6
 Unprocessed, raw animal-based treats, for example, contaminated pigs’ ears, are a risk of pathogen transmission.7-10
 Toxic food ingredients include:
x Chocolate x Macadamia nuts
x Onions, leeks, shallots, garlic, chives
x Grapes, raisins, currants and sultanas
x Xylitol (sweetener)
x Alcohol and raw yeast dough
x Caffeinated drinks, including coffee, tea and energy drinks
How many treats can I feed?

paragraphs.text: Treats include any food items that are given to your dog in addition to a complete and balanced diet.
 These include snacks, chews, supplements, and foods used to administer medication.
 They may be commercially available or home prepared using food intended for people.
 Treats should always make up less than 10% of a dog’s daily calorie intake.
 Maintaining an optimal weight is essential to supporting dog health and quality of life.
 For commercial treats, contact the manufacturer for calorie information if not stated on the label.
 Treats should never replace a meal – every dog needs a complete and balanced diet.
 Chat with your dog’s veterinary health care team to determine a suitable quantity and type of treat.
 Consider alternative ways of spending fun, quality time with your dog.
 Ensure that any treat offered is an appropriate size and shape to reduce the risk of choking.

 Treats must be safe and appropriate for your dog. The wrong treat, even if popular, can result in obesity1, trauma2, obstruction3 and even death.4 If your dog has a medical condition, dietary sensitivities, or is being fed a veterinaryprescribed diet, conventional treats may not be appropriate. Ask your veterinary healthcare team for advice if you are unsure what is suitable for your dog.
 Human food and table scraps can be unhealthy11 and potentially dangerous12 to dogs.
Treats should make up no more than 10% of a dog’s daily calorie intake. The following table identifies the maximum number of calories your dog should be consuming based on their current bodyweight.

* Based on a daily calorie requirement (kcal/day) for an average healthy adult dog in ideal body condition. Please speak to your veterinary healthcare team to determine your own dog’s daily energy requirement.
